newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Food, fuel prices jump in Kabul as afghani falls.
newsitem.headline: Food, fuel prices jump in Kabul as afghani falls.

text.p: Food and fuel prices have risen sharply in Afghanistan's war-shattered capital Kabul over the past few days as the shaky local currency, the afghani lost value, local traders said on Wednesday.
Prices of essential food items such as wheat flour have risen 13 per cent since Friday.
The price of petrol, which like most other commodities is imported from neighbouring Pakistan, has risen to 55,000 afghanis (about $2) for 4.5 litres (one gallon) from 47,000 afghanis last week.
The price rises come at the start of the Moslem holy month of Ramadan.
The main reason for the price rise is the decline of the afghani, which has lost more than 16 percent of its value over the past two days.

Local money dealers said the currency began falling after reports that false 10,000-afghani bills were being circulated by opponents of the ruling Taleban Islamic movement seeking to sabotage the monetary system.
The false notes are moved from opposition-held northern provinces to Pakistan via Pakistan's border district of Chitral and then sent to Taleban-ruled areas in bulk, dealers said.
They said the afghani gradually lost its value owing to the circulation of the new 10,000-afghani notes, most with similar serial numbers as old notes.
No comment on the situation was immediately available from the Taleban, the fundamentalist Islamic group which captured Kabul in late September from forces loyal to Rabbani.
Meagre incomes and the lack of job opportunities have made the life of Kabul's residents miserable.
"Nobody cares about us," said an old cobbler with a deep sigh. "The employment situation is not at all good, and if you have a job, the salary is not enough to forge ahead this damn life."
The number of vulnerable people in Kabul is rising sharply as war-displaced families from the Shomali valley, northeast of Kabul, flood the city seeking shelter.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and U.N. agencies are the main sources of hope for hundreds of thousands of such people in Kabul who are struggling against the winter cold.
And the falling value of the afghani is likely to further increase the hardship of Kabul residents at this time of year.
It is a tradition, particularly during Ramadan, for the rich to help the poor, but it is one that gains particular poignancy in Afghanistan.

After 17 years of war, many people are unable to afford sufficient food. The ICRC estimates that 57 percent of the population of Afghanistan are malnourished. The United Nations World Food Programme estimates that half of Kabul's population receive food aid of some sort.
